accepted.s: Special Drawing Rights (SDRs) are best described as which one of the following?
o: A short-term commercial loan granted by the IMF to private banks
A physical currency issued by the IMF for circulation among member countries
A compulsory contribution paid by members exclusively in gold
An interest-bearing international reserve asset existing as book-keeping entries
accepted.x: An SDR is an interest-bearing international reserve asset created by the IMF. It exists as accounting or book-keeping entries and is often described as ‘paper gold’.
accepted.tq: Choose the precise institutional definition rather than a familiar but incorrect physical-currency description.
accepted.sec: SDR - nature, form, basket, allocation, reserve tranche  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

accepted.s: The expression ‘paper gold’ in the context of the International Monetary Fund refers to:
o: Gold certificates issued by central banks
Reserve currencies held in physical form
Gold loans provided by the World Bank
accepted.x: Special Drawing Rights are popularly known as ‘paper gold’ because they are reserve assets recorded as accounting entries rather than physical gold.
accepted.tq: Discriminate between a popular descriptive term and physical forms of gold reserves.
accepted.sec: SDR - nature, form, basket, allocation, reserve tranche  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

accepted.s:
With reference to SDRs, consider the following statements:
1. The SDR was created in 1969 under the IMF’s First Amendment.
2. The proposal for the SDR was agreed in 1967.
3. Originally, 35 SDRs were equivalent to one ounce of gold.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
accepted.x: All three statements are correct. The SDR was agreed in 1967, formally created in 1969 under the IMF’s First Amendment, and was originally valued at 35 SDRs per ounce of gold.
accepted.tq: Separate the agreement date from the formal creation date and retain the numerical conversion.
accepted.sec: SDR - nature, form, basket, allocation, reserve tranche  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

accepted.s: Which one of the following correctly represents the currencies in the SDR basket since 1 October 2016?
o: US dollar, euro, renminbi, yen and pound sterling
US dollar, euro, rupee, yen and Swiss franc
US dollar, pound sterling, rupee, franc and yen
Euro, renminbi, rupee, Australian dollar and yen
accepted.x: Since 1 October 2016, the SDR basket comprises the US dollar, euro, Chinese renminbi, Japanese yen and pound sterling.
accepted.tq: Start with the sure currency pair and eliminate options containing currencies outside the stated basket.
accepted.sec: SDR - nature, form, basket, allocation, reserve tranche  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

accepted.s: The largest general allocation of SDRs, amounting to approximately SDR 456 billion or about US$650 billion, was made in:
accepted.x: The largest general SDR allocation was made in August 2021 and amounted to approximately SDR 456 billion, equivalent to about US$650 billion.
accepted.tq: Match the unusually large numerical allocation with its correct year.
accepted.sec: SDR - nature, form, basket, allocation, reserve tranche  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

accepted.s: The reserve tranche of an IMF member refers to:
o: The part of the member’s IMF quota paid in reserve assets and drawable without conditions
The portion of the IMF quota payable only in domestic currency
A compulsory gold loan extended by the member to other countries
The part of an SDR allocation that cannot be withdrawn
accepted.x: The reserve tranche is the portion of an IMF member’s quota paid in reserve assets, historically gold. It can be drawn at any time without conditions.
accepted.tq: Identify the correct IMF quota component by asking who can draw it and under what conditions.
accepted.sec: SDR - nature, form, basket, allocation, reserve tranche  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

accepted.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the transition from FERA to FEMA?
o: FERA 1969 was replaced by FEMA 2006, which came into force on 31 July 2006
FERA 1973 was replaced by FEMA 1997, which came into force on 1 April 1998
FERA 1999 was replaced by FEMA 1973, which came into force on 1 June 2000
FERA 1973 was replaced by FEMA 1999, which came into force on 1 June 2000
accepted.x: The restrictive Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1973 was replaced by the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999, which came into force on 1 June 2000.
accepted.tq: Use the law-year and commencement-date pair together to avoid swapping the two statutes.
accepted.sec: FERA to FEMA and rupee convertibility  [other exams, GROUP-II]

accepted.s: The proposal to replace FERA with a new foreign exchange management law was associated with which of the following?
accepted.x: The proposal for the new foreign exchange management framework was made in the 1997–98 Budget.
accepted.tq: Test the budget-year association directly, using nearby reform years as distractors.
accepted.sec: FERA to FEMA and rupee convertibility  [other exams, GROUP-II]

accepted.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Tarapore Committees:
1. The First Tarapore Committee was constituted in 1997.
2. The Second Tarapore Committee was set up in March 2006.
3. The Second Committee reported on 31 July 2006.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
accepted.x: All three statements are correct. The Tarapore Committees of 1997 and 2006 prepared roadmaps towards full capital account convertibility; the second committee reported on 31 July 2006.
accepted.tq: Check both the committee year and the distinct constitution and reporting dates.
accepted.sec: FERA to FEMA and rupee convertibility  [other exams, GROUP-II]

accepted.s: The Tarapore Committees were primarily associated with the roadmap towards:
accepted.x: The First and Second Tarapore Committees were associated with preparing a roadmap towards full capital account convertibility.
accepted.tq: Match the named committee with its specific policy objective rather than a broader exchange-policy term.
accepted.sec: FERA to FEMA and rupee convertibility  [other exams, GROUP-II]

accepted.s: Which of the following correctly states India’s position regarding rupee convertibility?
o: The rupee has full current account convertibility but only partial capital account convertibility
The rupee has neither current account nor capital account convertibility
The rupee has full capital account convertibility but partial current account convertibility
The rupee has full convertibility on both current and capital accounts
accepted.x: India has full current account convertibility, whereas capital account convertibility remains partial.
accepted.tq: Keep current-account and capital-account convertibility separate; the comparison is the key discriminator.
accepted.sec: FERA to FEMA and rupee convertibility  [other exams, GROUP-II]

accepted.s: The base year used for the Reserve Bank of India’s NEER index is:
accepted.x: The NEER index uses 2015–16 as its base year, represented as 100.
accepted.tq: Identify the exact base-year figure instead of confusing it with earlier economic-series base years.
accepted.sec: REER and NEER - meaning of a rise, base and weights  [other exams, GROUP-II]

accepted.s:
With reference to the Nominal Effective Exchange Rate (NEER), consider the following statements:
1. It is a trade-weighted average of the rupee against partner currencies.
2. A rise in NEER indicates appreciation of the rupee.
3. A rise in NEER generally makes imports cheaper and exports less competitive.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
accepted.x: All three statements are correct. NEER is trade-weighted, and its rise indicates rupee appreciation, which tends to reduce import costs but makes Indian exports less competitive.
accepted.tq: Trace the direction of appreciation through both import prices and export competitiveness.
accepted.sec: REER and NEER - meaning of a rise, base and weights  [other exams, GROUP-II]

accepted.s: Which one of the following best distinguishes REER from NEER?
o: NEER measures inflation while REER measures the fiscal deficit
REER is NEER adjusted for relative inflation
REER is NEER adjusted only for gold holdings
NEER is REER adjusted for reserve-tranche drawings
accepted.x: REER is obtained by adjusting NEER for relative inflation. It is considered a better indicator of external competitiveness, while a high REER suggests an overvalued rupee.
accepted.tq: Discriminate between the nominal index and its inflation-adjusted counterpart.
accepted.sec: REER and NEER - meaning of a rise, base and weights  [other exams, GROUP-II]

accepted.s: A high REER is generally interpreted as indicating that the rupee is:
o: Convertible only on the capital account
Fixed permanently to the US dollar
accepted.x: A high REER generally indicates an overvalued rupee. Since REER incorporates relative inflation, it is a better indicator of competitiveness than NEER alone.
accepted.tq: Apply the index interpretation to the policy meaning of an overvalued currency.
accepted.sec: REER and NEER - meaning of a rise, base and weights  [other exams, GROUP-II]

accepted.s: The Reserve Bank of India publishes trade-weighted NEER and REER indices based on:
accepted.x: The RBI publishes trade-weighted indices based on 40-currency and 6-currency baskets.
accepted.tq: Retain both components of the paired numerical fact instead of selecting a familiar-looking single basket.
accepted.sec: REER and NEER - meaning of a rise, base and weights  [other exams, GROUP-II]

accepted.s: During the rupee movement described for 2026, the rupee remained around which range against the US dollar, in the context of the West Asia crude shock and FPI selling?
accepted.x: The rupee was reported around ₹95–96 per US dollar through 2026 amid the West Asia crude shock and foreign portfolio investor selling.
accepted.tq: Link the exchange-rate range with the stated contemporaneous causes rather than using a historical rupee level.
accepted.sec: Universal angles

accepted.s: In response to the rupee slide in 2026, which combination of measures was associated with the Reserve Bank of India’s approach?
o: Repo-rate reduction, gold sales and abolition of FCNR(B) deposits
Swaps, FCNR(B) measures and retention of the repo rate at 5.25% for the fourth straight meeting
Capital controls, SDR cancellation and a fixed dollar peg
Complete capital account convertibility and withdrawal from the foreign exchange market
accepted.x: The RBI leaned on swaps and FCNR(B) measures while keeping the repo rate at 5.25% for the fourth straight meeting in August 2026.
accepted.tq: Combine the policy instrument, deposit measure and unchanged rate to identify the complete response.
accepted.sec: Universal angles

accepted.s: The first INR drawdown under the SAARC framework was made by:
accepted.x: The first INR drawdown under the SAARC framework was made by the Maldives in April 2026.
accepted.tq: Use the first-event and country-date combination as a three-part recall test.
accepted.sec: Universal angles

accepted.s: According to the stated September 2026 position, India’s foreign exchange reserves were approximately:
accepted.x: India’s reserves were reported at US$785.71 billion, making India the fourth-largest holder according to the stated September 2026 position.
accepted.tq: Match the exact reserve figure with its corresponding global rank.
accepted.sec: Universal angles

accepted.s: Deliberate undervaluation of a currency, as alleged in the case of China, is criticised as:
accepted.x: Deliberate undervaluation of a currency to gain trade advantages is criticised as currency manipulation.
accepted.tq: Match the policy criticism with the precise international-exchange term.
accepted.sec: Universal angles

accepted.s:
Arrange the following in chronological order:
A. Introduction of full current account convertibility in India
B. First Tarapore Committee
C. FEMA coming into force
D. Introduction of the rupee symbol
accepted.x: The correct sequence is full current account convertibility in 1994, the First Tarapore Committee in 1997, FEMA coming into force in 2000, and the rupee symbol in 2010.
accepted.tq: Fix the earliest and latest events first, then place the two intermediate reform milestones.
accepted.sec: Universal angles
